sentences.text: The ocean is salty because minerals have been washing into it for a very long time.
Rain falls on land and seeps into soil and rock.
Some minerals, including salts, dissolve. They mix into the water and are carried along.
Rivers and streams deliver that water to the sea.
When seawater evaporates, the water becomes vapor and leaves the minerals behind.
The salt does not float away with the clouds.
Over millions of years, this pattern made the ocean much saltier than most lakes and rivers.
The seafloor adds minerals too. In some places, seawater seeps into cracks, heats near hot rock, and returns full of dissolved minerals.
Those hot openings are called hydrothermal vents.
Salt is not added by fish, and it is not the leftover of one storm.
A salty taste comes from sodium and other dissolved minerals spread through the water.
If you boiled a pot of seawater, the water would steam away and a crust of salt would remain.
That small experiment is the same idea as evaporation across the ocean, only faster and much smaller.
Fresh rain still falls on the sea, but new minerals keep arriving, and evaporating water leaves salt behind.
The ocean's salt is a slow story written by water, rock, and time.

questions.prompt: What is this passage mostly about?

choices.text: How fish pour salt into the waves
Why rivers are saltier than the sea
How minerals collect in the ocean and stay there
How one storm made the ocean salty

questions.explanation: Rivers carry dissolved minerals to the sea, evaporation leaves them behind, and vents add more. The long buildup of salt is the main idea.

questions.prompt: In this passage, dissolve means what?

choices.text: To freeze into a hard crust
To float away inside a cloud
To sink as a whole rock
To mix into water so the solid seems to disappear into it

questions.explanation: The passage says minerals dissolve, then explains that they mix into the water and are carried along. That is the meaning.

questions.prompt: What are the hot openings on the seafloor called?

choices.text: Hydrothermal vents
River mouths
Salt crusts
Rain shadows

questions.explanation: The passage names the hot seafloor openings hydrothermal vents, after describing seawater that heats near hot rock.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't rain falling on the ocean make the sea fresh over time?

choices.text: Rain cannot fall on salt water
Minerals keep arriving, and evaporation leaves salt behind
Rivers carry only pure salt and no water
Clouds put the salt back into every lake

questions.explanation: The passage says fresh rain does fall on the sea. It also says minerals keep arriving and evaporating water leaves salt behind. Those two facts answer the puzzle.

questions.prompt: What happens first to many of the minerals that start on land?

choices.text: They form a crust in a cooking pot
They leave the ocean inside clouds
Rainwater dissolves them and rivers carry them to the sea
They heat up in hydrothermal vents

questions.explanation: On land, the passage starts with rain dissolving minerals. Rivers carry them next. Vents are a separate source, and the pot is only a comparison.
